body:
Atomic number identifies an element

The atomic number, represented by Z, is the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.

The atomic number determines the chemical identity of an element. Every hydrogen atom contains 1 proton, every carbon atom contains 6 protons and every oxygen atom contains 8 protons.

For a neutral atom, the number of electrons is also equal to Z. This is because its positive and negative charges must balance.

However, the number of neutrons is not determined by Z alone. Atoms of the same element may contain different numbers of neutrons.

Mass number counts nucleons

The mass number, represented by A, is the total number of protons and neutrons in an atom's nucleus.

Protons and neutrons are together called nucleons. Therefore:

\(A=Z+\text{number of neutrons}\)

Rearranging gives:

\(\text{number of neutrons}=A-Z\)

Because protons and neutrons are counted as individual particles, A and Z are always whole numbers.

Reading atomic notation

Atomic notation places the mass number at the upper left and the atomic number at the lower left of the element symbol. For example:

\({}^{23}_{11}\mathrm{Na}\)

This represents sodium-23. It has atomic number 11 and mass number 23.

Consequently, its nucleus contains 11 protons and 12 neutrons. If the atom is neutral, it also has 11 electrons.

One-step neutron calculation

An aluminium atom has atomic number 13 and mass number 27. Its number of neutrons is:

27 − 13 = 14 neutrons.

What changes when an atom becomes an ion?

A neutral sodium atom contains 11 protons and 11 electrons. When it loses 1 electron, it becomes Na+. The sodium ion contains 11 protons and 10 electrons.

For sodium-23, the number of neutrons remains 12 in both the neutral atom and the ion. Losing an electron does not alter the nucleus or the mass number.

Similarly, a neutral chlorine atom with atomic number 17 has 17 electrons. If it gains 1 electron, it becomes Cl−, with 18 electrons.

These examples lead to a useful distinction:

  • Atomic number: Depends on protons, not electrons.
  • Mass number: Depends on protons and neutrons, not electrons.
  • Ionic charge: Depends on the difference between proton and electron counts.

Determining the electrical charge

If an atom or ion contains 12 protons and 10 electrons, its net relative charge is +2. The excess of 2 positive charges identifies it as a doubly positive ion.

If an atom or ion contains 9 protons and 10 electrons, its net relative charge is −1. The extra electron produces a negative ion.

For a neutral atom, protons = electrons = Z. For an ion, protons = Z still holds, but the electron count changes.

Prelims focus

  • Z is the number of protons.
  • A is the sum of protons and neutrons.
  • The number of neutrons is A − Z.
  • Neutral atoms have equal numbers of protons and electrons.
  • Sodium-23 contains 11 protons and 12 neutrons.
  • Trap: Forming Na+ changes the electron count, not the atomic number.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class IX, Chapter 4, Structure of the Atom, sections 4.1, 4.2.4 and 4.5, printed pp. 46–49 and 52–53.]

pictures.alt: Sodium-23 has mass number 23 and atomic number 11. Forming Na+ reduces electrons from 11 to 10; both nuclei retain 11 protons and 12 neutrons.
pictures.caption: Atomic notation identifies protons and nucleons, while electrical charge determines electron count.

title: Atomic Number, Mass Number and the Composition of Atoms and Ions

body:
Isotopes are atoms of the same element

Isotopes are atoms of the same element that have the same atomic number but different mass numbers.

All isotopes of an element contain the same number of protons. However, they contain different numbers of neutrons. Since the number of protons is unchanged, the atoms remain members of the same chemical element.

The 3 familiar isotopes of hydrogen

Hydrogen provides a clear example of isotopes.

IsotopeProtonsNeutronsMass number
Protium101
Deuterium112
Tritium123

Protium is represented by hydrogen-1, deuterium by hydrogen-2 and tritium by hydrogen-3. All 3 have atomic number 1. Their nuclei differ only in neutron number.

Properties of isotopes

Neutral isotopes of the same element have the same number of electrons and generally have very similar chemical properties. Their masses differ, and some physical or nuclear properties may differ significantly.

For example, tritium is radioactive, whereas protium and deuterium are stable. This difference arises from the nature of their nuclei.

Isotopes are useful in several fields. At the level of basic general science, important examples include uranium-235 as a nuclear fuel, cobalt-60 in some forms of cancer radiotherapy, and iodine-131 in selected thyroid-related medical treatments.

Average atomic mass of an element

Many elements occur naturally as mixtures of isotopes. A tabulated atomic mass therefore reflects the weighted average of the masses of their isotopes, taking their relative abundances into account.

Chlorine has 2 important naturally occurring isotopes: chlorine-35 and chlorine-37. A common school-level example approximates their relative proportions as 3:1.

Using mass numbers as approximate isotope masses, the average is:

\(\frac{3\times35+1\times37}{4}=35.5\ \mathrm{u}\)

This explains the familiar approximate atomic mass of chlorine, 35.5 u. Modern high-precision tables give a value near 35.45 u because the actual isotope masses and natural abundances are more precise than the simplified school figures.

Average atomic mass is not the mass number of an individual atom. No chlorine atom has 35.5 nucleons.

Isobars are atoms of different elements

Isobars are atoms of different elements that have the same mass number but different atomic numbers.

Argon-40 and calcium-40 are isobars. Both have mass number 40, but argon has atomic number 18 while calcium has atomic number 20.

Argon-40 therefore has 18 protons and 22 neutrons. Calcium-40 has 20 protons and 20 neutrons. Their equal mass numbers do not make them isotopes because they are different elements.

Isotopes and isobars compared

FeatureIsotopesIsobars
Elements involvedSame elementDifferent elements
Atomic numberSameDifferent
Mass numberDifferentSame
Neutron numberDifferentDifferent
ExampleHydrogen-1 and hydrogen-2Argon-40 and calcium-40

Prelims focus

  • Isotopes have the same Z but different A.
  • Isobars have the same A but different Z.
  • Protium, deuterium and tritium have 0, 1 and 2 neutrons respectively.
  • Argon-40 and calcium-40 are isobars.
  • Chlorine's school-level average atomic mass is approximately 35.5 u.
  • Trap: Equal mass numbers do not imply that 2 atoms belong to the same element.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class IX, Chapter 4, Structure of the Atom, sections 4.5–4.6.1, printed pp. 52–54; NIST, Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for Chlorine, consulted 3 November 2026; US Department of Energy, National Isotope Development Center, Isotope Basics, consulted 3 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Hydrogen nuclei each contain 1 proton: protium has 0 neutrons, deuterium has 1, and tritium has 2. All have Z = 1; A is 1, 2 and 3.
pictures.caption: Hydrogen isotopes have the same proton number but different numbers of neutrons.

pictures.alt: Argon-40 has 18 protons and 22 neutrons; calcium-40 has 20 protons and 20 neutrons. Both nuclei contain 40 nucleons.
pictures.caption: Isobars have the same total nucleon count but different proton and neutron counts.

title: Isotopes, Isobars and Average Atomic Mass

body:
How electrons are arranged in shells

The electronic configuration of an atom describes the distribution of its electrons among the permitted energy levels or shells.

At this level, the shells are identified by the letters K, L, M and N, beginning with the innermost shell. They correspond to shell numbers 1, 2, 3 and 4.

The Bohr-Bury scheme states that the maximum number of electrons associated with a shell is given by:

\(2n^2\)

Here, n is the shell number. This gives the following theoretical shell capacities:

ShellShell numberMaximum electrons
K12
L28
M318
N432

For the first 20 elements, a useful simplified filling pattern is 2, 8, 8, 2 up to calcium. The outermost occupied shell contains no more than 8 electrons in this introductory model.

The third shell has a theoretical capacity of 18 electrons, but potassium and calcium begin occupying the fourth shell after the third contains 8 electrons. Therefore, potassium is 2,8,8,1, not 2,8,9, and calcium is 2,8,8,2, not 2,8,10.

Electronic configurations: atomic numbers 1–10

For a neutral atom, the atomic number is equal to its total number of electrons. The entries in an electronic configuration must add up to that number.

ZElementConfigurationSimple valency
1Hydrogen (H)11
2Helium (He)20
3Lithium (Li)2,11
4Beryllium (Be)2,22
5Boron (B)2,33
6Carbon (C)2,44
7Nitrogen (N)2,53
8Oxygen (O)2,62
9Fluorine (F)2,71
10Neon (Ne)2,80

Electronic configurations: atomic numbers 11–20

ZElementConfigurationSimple valency
11Sodium (Na)2,8,11
12Magnesium (Mg)2,8,22
13Aluminium (Al)2,8,33
14Silicon (Si)2,8,44
15Phosphorus (P)2,8,53
16Sulphur (S)2,8,62
17Chlorine (Cl)2,8,71
18Argon (Ar)2,8,80
19Potassium (K)2,8,8,11
20Calcium (Ca)2,8,8,22

The valencies in these tables are the simple school-level valencies predicted from the outer-shell arrangement. Some elements, including phosphorus and sulphur, can also show other valencies in particular compounds.

Valence electrons and chemical behaviour

The electrons in the outermost occupied shell are called valence electrons. They play an important role in chemical combination.

Sodium has configuration 2,8,1 and therefore 1 valence electron. It can lose that electron to form Na+, which has the stable shell arrangement 2,8.

Chlorine has configuration 2,8,7 and therefore 7 valence electrons. It can gain 1 electron to form Cl−, which has the arrangement 2,8,8.

Magnesium has 2,8,2 and commonly forms Mg2+ by losing 2 electrons. Oxygen has 2,6 and commonly forms O2− by gaining 2 electrons.

These examples connect electronic configuration to valency and, consequently, to the chemical formulas of simple compounds.

Why noble gases have valency 0

Helium has 2 electrons in its only shell. This is a complete first shell, called a duplet. Neon and argon have 8 electrons in their outermost shells, called an octet.

These full outer shells explain why noble gases generally show very little tendency to undergo ordinary chemical combination at the school level. Their usual valency is 0.

The special position of potassium and calcium

Potassium has atomic number 19 and calcium has atomic number 20. Their correct shell distributions are 2,8,8,1 and 2,8,8,2.

These configurations show an important limitation of applying the expression 2n2 as a simple instruction to fill each shell completely before starting the next. The expression gives a maximum shell capacity; it does not by itself determine the order in which all atomic energy levels are occupied.

Connecting the central concepts

The identity of an element depends on its atomic number, which equals its proton count. The mass number counts protons and neutrons. In a neutral atom, the proton count also determines the number of electrons, whose arrangement gives the electronic configuration.

The outer electrons help determine valency, which is useful for writing chemical formulas. Those formulas identify the particles or formula units whose masses can be calculated. The mole connects the amount of a substance to a definite number of particles. During ordinary chemical reactions, these particles rearrange while the total mass and numbers of each type of atom are conserved.

For a particular pure compound, the relative numbers of its constituent atoms remain fixed, giving a fixed composition by mass. Thus, atomic structure, chemical formulas, the mole concept and the laws of chemical combination describe connected aspects of the same subject.

Prelims focus

  • K, L, M and N shells have theoretical capacities of 2, 8, 18 and 32 electrons.
  • Sodium has electronic configuration 2,8,1.
  • Chlorine has electronic configuration 2,8,7.
  • Argon has electronic configuration 2,8,8 and usual valency 0.
  • Potassium is 2,8,8,1 and calcium is 2,8,8,2.
  • Trap: A shell's theoretical maximum capacity is not always the number of electrons it contains before the next shell starts filling.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class IX, Chapter 4, Structure of the Atom, sections 4.3–4.4, printed pp. 49–52; NCERT, Science, Class IX, Chapter 3, Atoms and Molecules, sections 3.1 and 3.4–3.5, printed pp. 31–33 and 37–42; Creative Chemistry, Electronic Configurations, first 20 elements, consulted 3 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Shell maxima are 2, 8, 18, 32, but potassium fills 2,8,8,1 and calcium fills 2,8,8,2: N starts while M contains 8.
pictures.caption: Potassium and calcium begin filling the fourth shell even though the third shell can hold more electrons.

pictures.alt: Revision map links proton count to electrons, valency and formulas, then branches into mass and particle counting and the laws of chemical combination.
pictures.caption: Atomic identity, electron arrangement, chemical formulas and particle counting form one connected system of ideas.

title: Electronic Configuration and Valency of the First 20 Elements
